claim: Requests to the AWS STS global endpoint (sts.amazonaws.com) are served in the same Region where the request originates when that Region is enabled by default and the Amazon DNS server resolves the name; requests from opt-in Regions or resolved by another DNS resolver are still served in US East (N. Virginia). AWS still recommends the Regional STS endpoints.
question: Where is a request to the STS global endpoint served today?

values.display: served in the same Region where the request originates
values.spoken: in the Region where the request starts

qualifiers.condition: Region enabled by default and Amazon DNS server

evidence.quote: Previously, all requests to the AWS STS global endpoint were served by a single AWS Region, US East (N. Virginia). Now in Regions enabled by default, requests to the AWS STS global endpoint are automatically served in the same Region where the request originates, rather than the US East (N. Virginia) Region. These changes will not be deployed to opt-in Regions.

Requests to the AWS STS global endpoint will continue to be served in US East (N. Virginia) Region if your request originated from opt-in Regions or if your request was resolved using a DNS resolver other than the Amazon DNS server.
We recommend that you use the appropriate AWS STS regional endpoints.
Previously, all requests to the STS global endpoint were served from the US East (N. Virginia) Region.

changed.was: Previously, all requests to the AWS STS global endpoint were served by a single AWS Region, US East (N. Virginia).

note: d099 current truth. Old trap: 'the STS global endpoint is a single point of failure in us-east-1'. The best answer is still: use Regional STS endpoints.

claim: On 2025-04-18 AWS STS began serving requests to the global endpoint (sts.amazonaws.com) in the same Region as the calling workload, for Regions enabled by default; before, all global endpoint requests were served from US East (N. Virginia).
question: What changed for the STS global endpoint in April 2025?

evidence.quote: AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) now automatically serves all requests to the global endpoint (sts.amazonaws.com) in the same AWS Region as your deployed workloads, enhancing resiliency and performance. Previously, all requests to the STS global endpoint were served from the US East (N. Virginia) Region.

This update is available in all AWS Regions that are enabled by default. No action is required from customers to benefit from these improvements. Any requests to the STS global endpoint from Regions not enabled by default (i.e. opt-in Regions) will continue to be served in US East (N. Virginia).

changed.was: Previously, all requests to the STS global endpoint were served from the US East (N. Virginia) Region.

note: d099. Older questions may treat the global endpoint as us-east-1 only.

claim: On 2026-07-30 the IAM Policy Simulator moved into the IAM console, replacing the standalone simulator site, and it can now include SCPs in a simulation.
question: Where do you run the IAM policy simulator since July 2026, and what can it now include?

evidence.quote: IAM Policy Simulator is now part of the IAM console, replacing the standalone simulator site, so you can test policies in the same place you manage your identities and policies. You can also now include SCPs in your simulation to test how your organization's SCP hierarchy interacts with identity and resource policies, and through the API, test how condition keys such as Region restrictions and tag requirements affect the outcome.
The standalone policy simulator console at https://policysim.aws.amazon.com/ is no longer maintained.

claim: On 2025-08-28 IAM added three global condition keys for network perimeters, aws:VpceAccount, aws:VpceOrgID and aws:VpceOrgPaths, which check that requests come through VPC endpoints owned by given accounts, organizations or OUs without listing each endpoint.
question: Which condition keys did IAM add in August 2025 for network perimeter controls?

evidence.quote: | [VPC endpoint condition keys for network perimeter controls](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html) | IAM now supports three new AWS global condition context keys for implementing scalable network perimeter controls: `aws:VpceAccount`, `aws:VpceOrgID`, and `aws:VpceOrgPaths`. These keys help ensure requests come through VPC endpoints owned by specific accounts, organizations, or organizational units, automatically scaling with your VPC endpoint usage without requiring policy updates when you create new endpoints. For more information, see [Establish permissions guardrails using data perimeters](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_data-perimeters.html). | August 28, 2025 |

To enforce network perimeter controls, we recommend that you use aws:VpceOrgID, aws:VpceOrgPaths, and aws:VpceAccount only if all services you want to restrict access to are currently supported. Using these condition keys with unsupported services can lead to unintended authorization results.

note: d105. Mention only. For wider service coverage the page recommends aws:SourceVpc and aws:SourceVpce.

claim: The global condition key aws:SourceVpcArn returns the ARN of the VPC to which the VPC endpoint of a request is attached; AWS recommends it instead of aws:SourceVpc when the target service supports it.
question: What does the aws:SourceVpcArn condition key check?

qualifiers.scope: per request made through a VPC endpoint

evidence.quote: Use this key to verify the ARN of the VPC that a request passed through using a VPC endpoint. This key returns the ARN of the VPC to which the VPC endpoint is attached.
AWS recommends to use aws:SourceVpcArn instead of aws:SourceVpc if aws:SourceVpcArn is supported by the service you are targeting.
Customers can use aws:SourceVpcArn in policies to ensure resources are only accessible from VPC endpoints in specific regions, helping enforce data residency requirements.

claim: Account access manager assigns the existing IAM roles in your AWS accounts to the users and groups of an IAM Identity Center organization instance; it works alongside Identity Center permission sets or on its own.

evidence.quote: Account access manager enables you to assign your existing IAM roles to the users and groups you have synchronized into IAM Identity Center from your corporate source of identities.

Previously, customers granting workforce access to AWS accounts could use one of two alternative access management approaches. They could federate users separately into each AWS account and define user permissions narrowly using the IAM roles in each AWS account. claim: IAM temporary delegation lets Amazon products and qualified AWS Partners request temporary, limited permissions in your account; after you approve, the provider acts on your behalf and the permissions expire automatically after the approved duration. Customers review and approve these requests but cannot create them.
question: What is IAM temporary delegation and who can create a delegation request?

qualifiers.condition: Amazon products and qualified AWS Partners only

evidence.quote: Temporary delegation enables Amazon and AWS Partners to request temporary, limited access to your account. Upon your approval, they can use delegated permissions to take actions on your behalf. Delegation requests define specific permissions to AWS services and actions that the product provider needs to deploy or configure resources in your AWS account. These permissions are only available for a limited time and automatically expire after the duration specified in the request.

Temporary delegation requests can only be created by Amazon products and qualified AWS Partners that have completed the feature onboarding process. Customers review and approve these requests but cannot create them directly.
This approach provides a more secure and streamlined experience by eliminating the need for you to create persistent IAM roles for such tasks, or perform them manually.

changed.was: create persistent IAM roles for such tasks, or perform them manually

note: d090. Launched 2025-11-19 (change feed). Low exam weight: mention once. A cross-account role with an external ID remains the classic third-party answer.

claim: IAM outbound identity federation lets AWS workloads call the STS GetWebIdentityToken API to get short-lived signed JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) and use them to access external services, so no long-term credentials of those services are stored.
question: How can an AWS workload authenticate to an external service without storing long-term credentials?

evidence.quote: IAM outbound identity federation enables your AWS workloads to securely access external services without storing long-term credentials. Your AWS workloads can request short-lived JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) from AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) by calling the GetWebIdentityToken API.

This allows customers to securely authenticate their AWS workloads with third-party cloud providers, SaaS providers, and self-hosted applications without using long-term credentials or implementing complex workarounds.

changed.was: using long-term credentials or implementing complex workarounds

note: d091. Launched 2025-11-19 (change feed). The opposite direction of the exam's usual federation (external IdP into AWS); mention only.
